item.title: Darwin, Racism, Canva, and AI
item.description:
Race and Ethnicity

Darwin, Racism, Canva, and AI

The new racism: A case study.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • AI-related technology has been shown to include implicit racist messaging.
  • In this day and age, something as innocent as using Canva can lead to deeply offensive and racist products.
  • Here, I describe a situation, connected with Darwin, in which racist messaging inadvertently created upset.
  • Modern technology amplifies racist and sexist worldviews; exactly what the world does not need right now.

Here is a story of something awful that happened last semester. I think we can all learn from it. I know that I did.

As Founding Director of the Evolutionary Studies (EvoS) program at the State University of New York at New Paltz, over the past two decades, I have learned a lot. The centerpiece of this program is an interdisciplinary speaker series that helps to bring important insights regarding life to our campus and to the broader community. Past speakers have addressed topics such as law, medicine, politics, literature, art, disease, and more—with a consistent focus on how Darwin's big ideas can help to shed light on so many issues of the human condition. Generally, I am proud of this program, including its diversity and its consistent capacity for helping to bring about insights for so many students, professors, and others who have an interest in learning more about how Darwin's ideas continue to advance our understanding of all facets of life.

As an evolutionary scientist, I have heard rumblings over the years of racist bias connected with some evolutionary thinking. As a full-on political progressive and humanist, these rumblings have never sat well with me. The Darwin that I learned about was famously abolitionist in his worldview (Desmond & Moore, 2014). And the standard learnings that I had gotten on this issue have consistently portrayed social Darwinism as a set of misinterpretations of Darwin's ideas to advance often-racist social agendas (see Wilson, 2019). It turns out that there is more to the story.

Last semester, an unprecedent-and-unfortunate situation took place. In an innocent, community-oriented effort to advertise a club event, a student group put out a flyer. Here is a snapshot from the flyer.

Source: Canva / AI-Generated

The number of people and offices who vetted this flyer was not insignificant. And this fact alone speaks to the implicit and systemic racism that surrounds our culture.

Don't see it? Look more closely. This image, generated by Canva, portrays evolution as a linear progression in a variant of what is called the "March of Progress." While I don't use this kind of image in my own work, I simply didn't see how deeply problematic this image was until it was shown to me how glaringly wrong it is. Not only does the march of progress ("lower" beings evolving into "higher" beings) not really characterize how natural selection actually works (natural selection is blind to concepts such as "lower" or "higher"—it "favors" attributes that are relatively adaptive over other attributes in certain ecological conditions), but when portrayed in a certain way, the march of progress can be conspicuously racist and sexist.

Look carefully at this image (which, at the time, was the #1 image that Canva produced on the prompting of "evolution" graphics). If you see monkeys turning into apes turning into a person of color turning into a white man, you would be seeing what I am now seeing. The second that a colleague of mine pointed this out, it became impossible to unsee. Of course, I felt terrible about the connotations—not to mention the fact that natural selection doesn't even work this way.

As renowned biologist Marlene Zuk (2010) pointed out clearly in her book Sex and the Scala Naturae, the march of progress concept is simply wrong. Evolution does not have a direction. There is no better or worse. Efforts to place people above other organisms are wildly misguided. Such efforts show a failed understanding of the process of natural selection. Further, efforts to create some kind of hierarchy with some groups of humans as above others, similarly show a lack of the basic logic that underlies natural selection. And such thinking can be profoundly dangerous.

Canva, which includes all kinds of AI-based algorithms (vis a vis the Canva Magic Studio AI feature), has, to my mind, demonstrated very clearly how leaning on AI has the capacity to amplify racism and sexism. The fact that the #1 image (in the winter of 2026) for evolution within the Canva environment was so obviously racist and sexist speaks volumes about the fact that modern technologies, and AI in particular, have the capacity to foster a culture of racism and sexism. As if that is what the world needs right now.

When the situation unfolded, the students who had used Canva to create that flyer sent a letter to the company several months ago, expressing concerns about the racism embedded in Canva content. Apparently, these students are still waiting for a reply back...

New Learnings

I was one of several faculty and staff members (along with several students) who, unfortunately, did not catch a glaring error. And I have been consistently remorseful for not catching it sooner—I still feel pretty wretched about it—even today. That said, there were actually some important learnings that came from open dialog with colleagues about this issue. Such learnings (for me) include the following:

  • AI-generated content has been shown to lean toward racism and sexism (c.f., Hofmann et al., 2024). This makes sense, unfortunately, as AI takes pre-existing content in its production of materials—and racist and sexist writings are steeped in what has been written by humans (largely by white male authors) across our checkered history.
  • As the world comes to lean more and more on AI and related technologies, we can only expect racist and sexist bias in written (and related) communications to become more prevalent.
  • When it comes to portraying evolution, the trope that is the march of progress is both inaccurate and dangerous. I think that evolutionary scholars should fully do away with it.
  • Darwin himself wasn't fully innocent when it comes to issues of race (e.g., several accounts of native peoples of South America that are described in The Descent of Man (Darwin, 1871) show indications of a racist worldview). This fact cannot be swept under the rug and I am happy to say that the EvoS program has plans to address this issue in upcoming programming.

Bottom Line

No matter where you stand politically, you likely would agree that the world is a mess right now.

Racism has a deep and disturbing place in the broader human historical experience. Modern communication technologies that lean strongly on AI, such as Canva, have the capacity to (perhaps unwittingly) harness and amplify racist (and sexist) worldviews and communications.

After processing the aforementioned situation regarding how a naive use of Canva technology unwittingly led to highly offensive, racist, and sexist messaging regarding a well-intentioned student-led event, I have concluded that publishing a piece on this issue (while not easy) may help people to pause and consider possible unintentional racist and sexist messaging—messaging that seems to be embedded in the world of AI and that is seeping more and more into everything with each passing second.

To my mind, the last thing that we need right now is to amplify racist and sexist worldviews.

As I've written about extensively in prior publications, while modern technology may have all kinds of upsides, the underbelly of the modern technological revolution is nothing short of abhorrent.

It is up to all of us to be mindful of these issues when utilizing modern technologies and AI content—in an effort to stamp out racism and sexism. Here is to a brighter future in which humans grab our own future by the reins. And not the robots.

Note: Thanks to Shannon Geher for her helpful editorial comments.

item.title: How to Create Your Best Good-Enough Day
item.description:
Self-Help

How to Create Your Best Good-Enough Day

Nietzsche's eternal recurrence: What if every day were Groundhog Day?

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Nietzsche's concept of eternal recurrence challenges us to step back and take stock of our lives.
  • For too many of us we fall into running on autopilot and to-do lists, losing sight of what brings us joy.
  • To create a day we are willing to live over and over is a matter of acting on our preferences and emotions.
Source: WikiImages/pixabay

In his book The Gay Science, the philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche presents the notion of eternal recurrence: If you were to live your life over and over for eternity, with all its joys, struggles, and tedium, could you accept it? Would that be a good-enough life? What is powerful about this question is that it forces you to step back and take stock of your everyday life—namely, is it good enough?

For all too many of us, we never have the time to step back and take a day’s pulse. But when I ask my clients to do precisely that, their everyday generally runs around a five—not a disastrous 1 nor an ecstatic 10. It’s not bad; it’s not great. It’s neutral, a shade under good-enough, because nothing bad happened. And if I ask what fills their lives, it’s, like for many of us, routines, to-do lists, and have-tos. By the end of the day, they're worn out. There are 8 or 9 days reserved for vacations and weekends, but even these are often heavily scheduled, and any unexpected disruptions can quickly quash the anticipated good times.

But what if you were willing to take Nietzsche’s question to heart and use it as a guide to create the best, good-enough days you would be willing to live over and over? Here are some ways to experiment with this idea:

Think about your ideal day

This is that classic question: If you had one day to live, what would you do besides saying goodbye to those you care about? Would you continue to go to work? Why? Would you go to some special place or do something with a special person? Why? Would you do something or experience something that has always been on your bucket list—skydive, conduct an orchestra, simply hang out with your family, or maybe have the greatest meal of your life?

What’s valuable about thinking this through is that it gives you a clue about what’s important and what’s most missing in your life. Even if what you desire seems out of reach—the travel, the experience—what is at its core that you need? Is it excitement, intimacy, novelty, or appreciation?

On your average good day now, notice what the best elements are

Going out to lunch with a colleague at work; reading bedtime stories to your son; or talking over dinner with your partner about your day. Maybe it’s the relaxation, quiet, and you-time you get from a hot bath at the end of the day.

This is a variation of the previous question, one that may tell you not what is missing but what you consider most important to keep.

Act on your preferences

Talking about preferences is to acknowledge two overlapping ideas: one concerns choices, the choices we make throughout the day that shape what unfolds (even following our routines is a choice). The other idea is that we can use our emotions as information—what we want or don’t want, what we prefer or desire, no matter how small. For example, we might want something different for lunch, or a change in our post-dinner routine with our family. Acting on your preferences starts with slowing down, stepping back, and asking yourself what your feelings and gut are telling you right now. Whatever comes to mind, go with it, no matter how minor it seems.

Source: caroloscuellito87/pixabay

Change your perspective

Asking people with depression to write down what they appreciate and are grateful for, no matter how small, has been shown to reduce feelings of depression. By shifting their perspective, they rewire their brains and improve their mood.

The same can work for you, especially if your behavioral choices throughout the day are limited for good reasons. Replace bold actions with subtle shifts in attitude and attention—notice the beauty of a sunset or the kindness of a stranger. If what you expect you will always find, and if what you think about you will become, experiment with changing your expectations and thoughts to see what happens.

The theme is that moving intentionally from action to action, choosing what you give your attention to, and using your emotions as a guide — rather than the shoulds, the have-tos, or unconscious behaviors — are the keys to creating a good-enough everyday life, one you’re willing to repeat.

Ready to give it a try?
